opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think that's actually one of the most natural workflows, and it's one I use myself all the time. Deep Research works best when you give it a pretty well-specified question. It's going to go off and spend five, ten, twenty minutes reading a lot of sources, so the more precisely you can say what you care about, the more useful the report you get back. But the catch is that when you're new to a topic, you often don't know what the right question is. You don't know the vocabulary, you don't know where the interesting debates are, you don't know which dimensions matter.

So what I'll often do is start with a regular conversational model and just kind of think out loud with it. I'll say, "I'm trying to understand X, here's roughly why I care about it, what are the main things I should be asking?" And it'll help me map out the space: these are the key subtopics, these are the terms people use, these are the tradeoffs that experts argue about. That back-and-forth is fast and cheap, so you can iterate a few times until you have a much sharper sense of what you actually want to know.

Then once I've got that, I'll turn it into a more detailed prompt for Deep Research: here's the specific question, here's the context, here's the kind of sources I trust, here's the format I want the answer in. And the difference in output quality is pretty dramatic compared to just firing off a vague one-liner.

And honestly, Deep Research itself already does a little of this. It'll often ask you a few clarifying questions before it kicks off, because we found that a little bit of upfront scoping makes a big difference. But I think of the conversational model as the brainstorming partner and Deep Research as the analyst you hand the brief to. Using them together, where one helps you figure out what to ask and the other goes and does the heavy lifting, is where a lot of the value is.

r001.rationale: The response suggests asking a conversational model what to ask and using the exchange to refine the topic, but it does not say to have the model ask the user questions.

r002.rationale: It describes using a regular conversational model to sharpen the question, then turning it into a detailed prompt for Deep Research.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think this is actually one of the more underrated parts of the whole workflow. When you sit down to kick off a Deep Research task, the quality of what you get back is pretty tightly coupled to the quality of the question you ask. And the problem is that the situations where you most want deep research are often exactly the situations where you don't know enough about the topic to ask a good question yet. You don't know what the right terminology is, you don't know what the important sub-questions are, you don't know what the trade-offs are that people in the field actually argue about.

So what I find myself doing, and what I think a lot of people are converging on, is using a conversational model as a kind of scoping step before the research step. You just start talking to it. You say, "Hey, I'm trying to understand X, I don't really know anything about it, here's roughly why I care." And the back-and-forth does a few useful things. It surfaces the vocabulary, so you learn what the field actually calls the thing you're vaguely gesturing at. It helps you figure out what you actually want to know versus what you think you want to know. A lot of the time my initial question is too broad, or it's secretly three different questions, and the conversation helps me pull those apart. And it helps you figure out the constraints. Like, am I looking for the academic consensus, or am I looking for what practitioners are actually doing, or am I trying to make a specific decision and I need the research to be shaped around that decision?

And then there's a nice handoff. Once you've had that conversation, you can basically ask the model, "Okay, given everything we just talked about, write me the research brief." And now you've got a prompt for Deep Research that's much more specific, that has the right framing, the right terms, maybe even a list of sub-questions to investigate, and some notes on what to prioritize or ignore.

I think the way to think about it is that the conversational model is cheap and fast and interactive, and the deep research agent is expensive and slow and runs on its own for a while. So you want to spend the cheap, fast cycles getting the question right before you spend the expensive cycle actually answering it. It's a bit like talking through a problem with a colleague before you go off and spend a day in the library. The conversation is where the problem gets defined, and then the research is where it gets answered.

r001.rationale: The response recommends a back-and-forth to scope the topic, but does not say to prompt the model to ask the user questions.

r002.rationale: It describes using a conversational model to refine the question and produce a research brief before starting Deep Research.

astra-6.text:
I think one of the hardest parts of doing research in an area you don’t know much about is figuring out what question to ask. You have some vague thing you want to understand, but you don’t have the vocabulary or know which distinctions matter yet.

A conversational model can help you work through that. You can say, “Here’s what I’m trying to figure out. What am I missing? What would you ask me to clarify?” And through that back-and-forth, you start to identify the question that would actually be useful to answer.

Then you can take that more precise question into Deep Research. So I see the conversation as a way to develop the research brief: what you’re trying to learn, why you care, and what would make the result useful. That’s especially valuable when you’re not yet knowledgeable enough to write a good brief yourself.

r001.rationale: It suggests asking the conversational model what needs clarification and says the back-and-forth helps identify a useful research question.

r002.rationale: It describes developing a research brief through conversation before using Deep Research, but does not specify that the conversational model is smaller.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one of the hardest parts of doing research in an area you don’t know much about is figuring out what question to ask. You have some vague thing you’re trying to understand, but you don’t necessarily have the vocabulary or know which distinctions matter.

A conversational model can help you work through that. You can say, “Here’s what I’m trying to accomplish. What am I missing? What would you need to know to investigate this?” And through that back-and-forth, you can get to a much more precise question, with some context about what a useful answer would look like. Then you can hand that to Deep Research. So the conversation becomes a way to develop the research brief, instead of expecting yourself to write the perfect prompt upfront.

r001.rationale: It suggests asking a conversational model what is missing and what it needs to investigate, then using that back-and-forth to refine the question.
